PA-2025-HB1006.s: The law updates milk testing and sampling rules under Pennsylvania’s Milk Marketing Law. It lets certified testers and certified weighers and samplers hold their certificates for up to two years instead of one, and it changes some fee references to the Milk Marketing Fee Act. People who test, weigh, or sample milk for dealers would be affected, and the law takes effect 60 days after approval.

PA-2025-HB1098.s: This act creates a program in the Pennsylvania Commission on Crime and Delinquency to help investigate and prosecute internet crimes against children. It lets the commission give grants to police and prosecutor task forces, support training, and add to other state or federal funding. It took effect immediately and was approved as Act No. 71 of 2026.

PA-2025-HB1345.s: The bill would make Medical Assistance cover treatments for menopause for eligible people in Pennsylvania. It would include FDA-approved drugs and devices, behavioral therapy, and treatment for menopause caused by a hysterectomy. The state would need federal approval before this coverage starts.

PA-2025-HB1346.s: The bill would require health insurance plans in Pennsylvania to cover hormone and non-hormone treatment for menopause symptoms. It would include FDA-approved drugs and devices, behavioral therapy, and treatment for menopause caused by a hysterectomy. The coverage would follow the plan’s normal rules on medical need, cost-sharing, and review, and it would apply at different times depending on when a plan is filed, issued, or renewed.

PA-2025-HB1633.s: The bill would let certain cities set up shared electric low-speed scooter programs with private scooter companies. It sets rules for where scooters can be used, how fast they can go, age limits, lights at night, insurance, reports, and fines for rule breaks. It also says these shared scooters would not need title or registration papers and would not count as motor vehicles.

PA-2025-HB1704.s: The law changes Pennsylvania rules for selling homes by adding flood-related details to property disclosure forms. Sellers must tell buyers about known flood risk factors and, if known, how many times and when the home had flood damage. The Insurance Department must post flood risk and flood insurance information on its website, and the new rules take effect in 60 days.

PA-2025-HB1827.s: The bill would require medical assistance and health insurance plans in Pennsylvania to cover screening, prevention, and treatment for osteoporosis for people who have reached menopause. It includes bone density testing, certain medicines and devices, and some prevention steps like dietary supplements, physical therapy, and weight training or personal training services. The new rules would apply to some plans when filed or renewed on or after the set dates in the bill, and the act would take effect in 90 days.

PA-2025-HB1935.s: The act changes Pennsylvania’s terroristic threats law. It would require people convicted under that law to pay restitution for evacuation costs and related response costs, and it lets courts order payment for supplies, equipment, wages, and other costs tied to the event. It also adds a sentencing guide for threats against schools and colleges, and it takes effect in 60 days.

PA-2025-HB1972.s: The law changes the rules for public adjusters in Pennsylvania. It raises the bond they must carry to $40,000, sets fee limits at 10% for catastrophe claims and 15% for other insurance claims, and bars fees before a claim is settled. It also adds rules on disclosures, referrals, licensing checks, and other limits on what adjusters and related businesses may do.

PA-2025-HB2014.s: The law changes Pennsylvania’s child labor rules for 14- and 15-year-olds who are in volunteer fire companies. It lets them do training or other allowed emergency service activities until 10 p.m. if they have written permission from a parent or legal guardian. The law took effect 60 days after it was signed.

PA-2025-HB2023.s: The bill would change state landlord-tenant law about eviction after a court order for possession of a property. It would let a justice of the peace delay carrying out the eviction during certain severe weather, such as freezing temperatures, winter storms, hurricanes, tropical storms, or extreme heat, for tenants enrolled in certain aid programs. After the bad weather ends, the eviction would have to be completed within five days, and the act would take effect 60 days after it becomes law.

PA-2025-HB2047.s: The bill would create a Local News Fellowship Program in Pennsylvania to place early-career journalists at approved local newsrooms. It would have a state education system office, or another designated state institution, run the program, choose fellows and host newsrooms, and report on results each year. Fellows would get pay, training, and mentoring, and the program would start 60 days after enactment.

PA-2025-HB2048.s: The bill would create the Pennsylvania Civic Information Consortium, a public nonprofit that would give grants to local news and civic information projects across the state. It would focus on underserved communities, protect editors from outside control, and require public reports, meetings, and a public website with grant info. It also sets up a 15-member board and calls for a plan for long-term funding after a pilot period.

PA-2025-HB2135.s: The bill would require employers to make reasonable changes for workers with pregnancy, childbirth, menopause, or related medical needs, unless it would cause major difficulty or cost. It would also bar employers from forcing leave, denying job chances because of a needed accommodation, or retaliating against workers who ask for one. Employers would have to give written notice of these rights to new workers, current workers, and workers who say they are pregnant or in menopause. The act would take effect 60 days after it becomes law.

PA-2025-HB2227.s: This act became law and names many bridges and highway sections across Pennsylvania for local people, veterans, firefighters, and other honorees. It also creates the Pennsylvania and National Medal of Honor Highway. The Department of Transportation must put up and keep signs showing the new names, and the law took effect 60 days after enactment.

PA-2025-HB2336.s: This law adds work zone safety to driver training and testing in Pennsylvania. Teens under 18 who want a junior driver's license must show they printed or viewed state materials on distracted driving and unsafe driving in work zones. The driver's manual and the written test must also cover how to drive safely in a work zone, and the law takes effect 60 days after approval.

PA-2025-HB2437.s: The law changes how some oil and gas fee money can be used for bridge projects in Pennsylvania counties. It lets counties use these funds to improve county or municipal bridges, even if the bridge does not qualify for federal aid, and lets first- or second-class counties use some money for bridges owned by a public transit authority. It takes effect in 60 days.

PA-2025-HB2464.s: This law updates parts of Pennsylvania’s insurance code and makes editorial changes. It changes some health insurance terms and references, including rules tied to medical assistance, children’s health coverage, long-term care, and prescription coverage. It also says it takes effect right away.

PA-2025-HB2474.s: The law updates child abuse rules by adding more sex-related crimes, including unlawful sharing of an intimate image and sexual abuse of children, to the kinds of acts that must be reported. It also requires certain staff to report suspected child abuse right away, tell the person in charge, and help with the investigation. Mandated reporters must also report suspected child sexual abuse material or AI-made child sexual abuse material, and the new law takes effect in one year.

PA-2025-HB2517.s: The bill would change the penalties for strangulation in Pennsylvania. It would make strangulation a second-degree felony in most cases, and a first-degree felony if it happens while the defendant is under certain protection orders, uses an instrument of crime, or has a past conviction for strangulation or a similar offense. It would take effect 60 days after it becomes law.

PA-2025-HB2519.s: The bill would require police to give a verbal or written warning to a person they believe may have been strangled. The warning would explain that strangulation can cause serious injury or death, even without visible signs, and would urge quick medical care. Police would also have to record whether they gave the warning, and the law would take effect 60 days after passage.

PA-2025-HB2545.s: The bill would require health insurance plans in Pennsylvania to cover vaginal estrogen for treating menopausal symptoms and for preventing urinary tract infections. It would apply to plans issued or renewed after the law takes effect, and it would cover FDA-approved drugs, devices, and combination products used to provide vaginal estrogen. The coverage could still be subject to plan rules like medical need checks, cost sharing, and review. The act would take effect 90 days after passage.

PA-2025-HB2555.s: Pennsylvania Act 88 of 2026 changes animal law rules for horses and other equines sold by a dealer. It requires a negative equine infectious anemia test, or a health inspection paper, microchip, tattoo, or brand as allowed, and it exempts foals under 6 months old if they are with their mother and she tested negative. Dealers must keep sale and health records for at least two years, and the act takes effect in 90 days.

PA-2025-HB2584.s: The bill would require the state Public Utility Commission to create and keep a public, searchable database of the utility rates it oversees. The database would include rate increase requests and at least 20 years of records, and it would be updated within 10 days after a new request is received. The commission could hire a third party to run the database, and the act would take effect immediately.

PA-2025-HB2593.s: The bill would require the state Health Department to run a public education campaign on prostate health and prostate cancer screening. It would share plain-language information on risk factors, screening tests, signs, and early treatment, and it would reach people through public ads, community forums, health offices, providers, and other groups. The campaign would also have materials in English, Spanish, Vietnamese, Mandarin Chinese, and other languages the department chooses, and it would be funded by a new state fund for this purpose.

PA-2025-HB2674.s: The bill would change the state’s public utility law by updating who counts as a public utility. It would add a new definition for a “commercial data center” and say some data centers are not public utilities if selling power to the grid is only a side part of their business. It would also make some resort water and sewer service and certain rail lines owned by local authorities count as public utilities for limited safety rules. The act would take effect in 60 days.

PA-2025-HB2706.s: The bill would create a Pennsylvania tax credit for resident individuals who already claim the federal child and dependent care credit. The credit would apply to work-related care costs, with limits of $3,000 for one qualifying person or $6,000 for two or more, and it could be refunded if the credit is more than the person owes in state tax. It would also repeal an older Fiscal Code section and take effect right away.

PA-2025-HB2771.s: The bill would set rules for automated license plate reader systems, which use cameras and software to read plate numbers. It would limit their use mostly to law enforcement and some parking or secured-area uses, require training, and add penalties for breaking the rules. It would also require captured data to be kept secure, kept private, and destroyed on a set schedule, and it would take effect six months after enactment.

PA-2025-HB2790.s: The bill would add rules for video streaming services in Pennsylvania. It would bar ads from having louder audio than the video they play with, and it lets people file complaints with the Attorney General’s consumer protection office. If a service breaks the rule, the Attorney General could seek a civil penalty of up to $5,000 for each violation and other court relief. The act would take effect in one year.

PA-2025-HB2826.s: The bill would create a state fund and a cancer screening program for eligible firefighters in Pennsylvania. It would pay for screening exams, like blood tests, ultrasounds, lung CT scans if needed, and skin checks, with screenings available at least twice a year in each region and once every three years for each eligible firefighter. The measure would also keep the health records private and take effect 60 days after it becomes law.

PA-2025-HB2865.s: The bill would update rules for dyed diesel fuel in Pennsylvania. It would require notices on certain sales and pumps, and it would keep dyed diesel out of motor vehicles on public highways unless federal law or a presidential executive order allows it. It would also change penalties and take effect right away.

PA-2025-HB2867.s: The bill would give extra LIHEAP payments to households that qualify for the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program, based on their expected cash and crisis benefits for the 2026-2027 season. It would also give a one-time $200 emergency utility payment to households with income at or below 250% of the federal poverty guidelines, but a household could not get both payments. The state would move $500 million from the Budget Stabilization Reserve Fund to pay for these costs, and the act would take effect in 60 days.

PA-2025-HB2868.s: The bill would lower the civil penalty from $500 to $100 for some vehicle owners or registrants who choose to pay a fee instead of serving a registration suspension. They would also have to pay the restoration fee and show proof of financial responsibility, which means car insurance or other required coverage. The choice could be used no more than once in a 12-month period, and the act would take effect in 60 days.

PA-2025-HB2869.s: The bill would let people deduct money they put into a Trump account from state taxable income on their yearly personal income tax return. The deduction would have an annual cap based on the federal gift tax exclusion, and it could not make taxable income less than zero. It would apply to tax years starting after December 31, 2026, and would take effect right away.

PA-2025-HB2870.s: The bill would change how Pennsylvania sales tax is rounded by using a new set of rounding rules based on the tax amount’s second decimal place. It would also require the state to study the revenue difference from that rounding and send that amount each year, if over zero, from the General Fund to the Public School Employees’ Retirement System account. The money would be used to help cover the system’s unfunded liabilities, and the act would take effect in 60 days.

PA-2025-HB2881.s: The bill would add a voluntary survey for resident hunting license applicants asking when the statewide regular firearms deer season should start, with answers limited to the Monday or Saturday after Thanksgiving. The game commission would post and report the results, and the most chosen answer would set the opening day for 10 hunting license years at a time. It would also make it illegal for someone to submit or change another person’s survey answer without legal authority, and it would take effect in 60 days.

PA-2025-HB2882.s: The bill would bar Pennsylvania officials from helping with out-of-state extradition, subpoenas, or other legal actions against medical providers over health care services that are lawful in Pennsylvania. It would also block state courts and licensing boards from enforcing out-of-state judgments, orders, or discipline based on those services, with a stated exception for medical malpractice claims under Pennsylvania law. The bill covers doctors, nurses, hospitals, and other health care providers, and it would also protect related patient and medical information from being shared with out-of-state authorities in these cases.

PA-2025-HB2883.s: The bill would bar the use of PFAS chemicals, a group of long-lasting man-made chemicals, in pesticides for most uses. It would also require the Department of Agriculture to make and keep a public list of PFAS pesticides, notify applicators, and stop registering new ones for sale after set time periods. The ban would cover health care facilities, schools, day care centers, residential lawn care, and commercial mosquito spraying, with an exception if the secretary finds a use is unavoidable for health, safety, or society's function.

PA-2025-HB2884.s: The bill would change the Keystone Scholars Grant Program and create a new Matching Trump Account Grant Program Account in the Treasury Department. It would use state money to match the federal first deposit in an eligible child’s Trump Account for children born after December 31, 2018, and families would be told about the program and could opt out. The account could get up to $100 for each child born in the state in a fiscal year, and the new funding rule would end on December 31, 2029. The act would take effect in 60 days.

PA-2025-HB36.s: This law updates the State Inspector General office rules in Pennsylvania. It adds a definition for an "enforcement officer" and lets those officers carry firearms while doing their official work if they follow office rules and finish required firearms training. It took effect right away.

PA-2025-HB369.s: Makes changes to the rules for land banks in Pennsylvania by updating the words used to define "land bank jurisdiction" and "municipality." It expands who can count as a municipality for these land bank rules and lets two or more municipalities use a shared agreement to set up and run a land bank. The act takes effect in 60 days.

PA-2025-HB507.s: The bill would require the state health department to test samples of baby food made in Pennsylvania for toxic heavy metals like arsenic, lead, cadmium, and mercury. It would set limits on how much of these metals can be in baby food sold in the state and require labels showing the test results. The bill says it would take effect one year after enactment.

PA-2025-HB559.s: The bill would add a new term for a place that has never had certain liquor licenses, or has not been used for a non-license business for at least three years. It would change how the Liquor Control Board handles some new license applications and transfers to these places, including hearings and nearby resident testimony. It would also let distributor license holders sell malt or brewed beverages in any amount for off-site use, and allow refillable growlers.

PA-2025-HB69.s: Pennsylvania Act 61 of 2026 became law and changes the cancer drug repository program into a prescription drug repository program. It lets approved pharmacies accept certain unused prescription drugs and give them to indigent patients if the drugs meet set safety rules. The State Board of Pharmacy must issue rules, post a public list of approved pharmacies, and send an annual report to lawmakers. The act takes effect in 60 days.

PA-2025-HB71.s: The law updates safety rules for towed vehicles in Pennsylvania. When two vehicles are joined by certain hitch types, they must also use two safety chains or cables of equal length that are strong enough for the weight being towed and crossed to help keep the tow bar from falling if it comes loose. It takes effect 60 days after approval.

PA-2025-HR672.s: The resolution would ask the federal government to condemn rioting and civil unrest in France and other parts of Europe. It would also express support for the people of France and other European allies, and say Pennsylvania stands for secure borders, the rule of law, and protecting property and rights. Copies would be sent to U.S. and Pennsylvania officials, including the French ambassador to the United States.

PA-2025-HR673.s: The resolution would ask the Joint State Government Commission to study how immigrant detention centers in Pennsylvania could be turned into community-focused projects. The study would look at the effects on local areas, ways to involve residents and groups in the process, and rules for getting state transition grant funds. It would also review possible funding sources and report back to the House within 12 months.

PA-2025-HR674.s: The House would recognize November 20, 2026, as "Transgender Day of Remembrance" in Pennsylvania. A resolution is a formal statement by lawmakers. It would honor transgender people lost to violence and call attention to violence against transgender Pennsylvanians.

PA-2025-SB1014.s: Pennsylvania enacted a law that requires schools to adopt a bell-to-bell policy for student mobile devices by the start of the 2026-2027 school year. The policy must bar device use during the school day on school property, set rules for possession, and include exceptions for certain medical, disability, language, and limited teacher-directed uses. Schools must give parents contact info and emergency alert details, post the policy online, and the state education department must report on effects on student discipline, mental health, attendance, and grades.

PA-2025-SB1217.s: Pennsylvania Act 107 of 2026 names many roads, bridges, an interchange, and a roundabout across the state in honor of veterans, public officials, and other people. It also orders the state transportation department to put up signs on the bridge named for Lieutenant Colonel Kenneth O. Hunter. The act takes effect 60 days after approval.

PA-2025-SB1260.s: The act creates a state licensing system for electrical contractors, electricians, residential electricians, apprentice electricians, and probationary electricians in Pennsylvania. It also sets up a State Board of Electrical Licensure to issue and manage licenses, make rules, keep a public registry, and handle fees, fines, and penalties. The law became Act No. 108 of 2026.

PA-2025-SB1334.s: The law updates Pennsylvania’s medical practice rules and adds new licenses for medical imaging professionals, radiation therapists, radiologist assistants, and trainees. It sets education, exam, age, and character rules for these jobs, and says some of these workers may perform certain imaging or therapy tasks under set limits or supervision. It also changes rules for several other licensed health jobs and removes older rules on some radiologic procedures and training.

PA-2025-SB1372.s: This act requires the state Human Services Department to make a yearly report on its inspections, investigations, and enforcement actions for child care centers, group child care homes, family child care homes, and child residential and day treatment facilities. The report must also cover complaints, child care payments made with taxpayer money, improper payments found, and money recovered, and it must be posted online and sent to key lawmakers by January 1 each year. It also sets carbon monoxide alarm standards for child care centers and family child care homes and took effect 60 days after passage.

PA-2025-SB1403.s: The bill would change rules for ambulance drop-off sites, called receiving facilities, and let the health agency set more types of places that can take patients, including help for people in a behavioral health or substance use crisis. It would also require payment rules for ambulance treatment and transport, so insurers, Medicaid managed care plans, and CHIP managed care plans pay the emergency service amount when a patient is taken to a receiving facility. The act would take effect 180 days after it becomes law.

PA-2025-SB1410.s: Now that it is law, this act bars state and local government contracts from including certain terms, such as forcing them to cover another party’s legal costs, use binding arbitration, or follow another state’s laws. It also blocks terms that would require them to pay extra interest or late fees beyond what state rules allow. Any banned term in a covered contract would be void, and the rest of the contract would still count. It takes effect in 60 days and applies to new, changed, or renewed contracts after that date.

PA-2025-SB1415.s: The bill would raise some penalties for harming or neglecting care-dependent people, including making certain neglect and abuse crimes felonies instead of misdemeanors. It would also make institutional sexual assault by a caretaker against a care-dependent person a more serious felony. The act would take effect 60 days after passage.

PA-2025-SB1485.s: The act changes the rules for racing licenses in Pennsylvania by expanding background checks for people applying to work in horse racing. It requires fingerprint-based criminal history checks for applicants in jobs tied to horse care, racing, wagering systems, security, and racing management, including many named roles like trainers, jockeys, stewards, and veterinarians. It became Act No. 116 of 2026 and took effect right away.

PA-2025-SB1488.s: The bill would let skill games be used in Pennsylvania for a temporary period. It would make the manufacture, sale, lease, distribution, repair, possession, placement, operation, and play of these games lawful, and people would not need a license or permit just for those acts. It would also block taxes or fees under this title from applying only because of skill game use. The temporary rule would end on April 13, 2027, and the bill would take effect right away.

PA-2025-SB1497.s: The bill would change Pennsylvania rules for business corporations and limited liability companies. It adds new definitions for election and ballot question activity, and it rewrites the power rules so these businesses could not use their general powers to support or oppose candidates, parties, or ballot questions. It also makes related wording and editorial changes in Title 15.

PA-2025-SB1499.s: The bill would change child welfare rules for kinship foster parents and family finding. It would update who counts as a relative or kin, require agencies to look for and notify relatives after a child is removed from home, and change what must be kept in the child’s case plan. It would also set clearer clearance checks and approval rules for kinship foster parents and spell out payment and public assistance rules for them.

PA-2025-SB1500.s: The bill would let a court, when someone willfully ignores a custody order, temporarily change the physical custody schedule. That change could give the child extra parenting time to make up for time lost with the other parent. It would apply in child custody cases, and it would take effect in 60 days.

PA-2025-SB1501.s: The bill would create the Pennsylvania Office of Freedmen Affairs in the state executive branch. The office would help some residents document family ties to enslaved people, study past unfilled promises from the Reconstruction era, and suggest policy ideas on housing, taxes, education, and other support for that group. It could take federal grants or private donations allowed by law, and the act would take effect 60 days after it becomes law.

PA-2025-SB1505.s: The bill would bar Pennsylvania schools from using artificial intelligence, chatbots, or generative AI to provide mental health or counseling services to students. It would also stop AI suppliers from contracting with schools for systems meant to act like a school psychologist, counselor, or social worker. School mental health staff could still use AI for office tasks, and the bill would take effect in 60 days.

PA-2025-SB1506.s: The bill would set rules for digital games sold in Pennsylvania. It would require game operators to give notice before stopping key online services and to offer a way to keep using the game, a refund, or other support. It would also set civil fines for violations and says the act would take effect in 60 days.

PA-2025-SB1507.s: The bill would make it illegal to use certain AI price-setting tools that rely on nonpublic competitor data, and it would also bar the use of common AI to set prices for goods or services sold in Pennsylvania. It would let the Attorney General investigate and bring cases, and it would let buyers who lose money sue for damages. The bill also sets criminal fines and says it would take effect right away.

PA-2025-SB1508.s: The bill would let authorized highway workers and emergency responders use emergency LED warning lights as extra warning devices in work zones and emergency response areas. It would also require drivers to yield when nearing those lights and would add rules for how the lights must be built and placed, such as being blue, rechargeable, and visible from 2,000 feet. A driver who does not yield could get a summary offense, a fine, and have to pay to replace any damaged device. The act would take effect in 60 days.

PA-2025-SB1509.s: The bill would change Pennsylvania child custody rules for grandparents and great-grandparents who seek partial or supervised custody. It would add or change when they can ask a court for custody, including cases involving a deceased parent or a child who lived with them for a set time and was then removed. It would also update what judges must consider in these custody cases, and the act would take effect in 60 days.

PA-2025-SB205.s: This law changes how some highway maintenance money can be used in counties. It lets counties use certain state funds for building and fixing bridges owned by towns and cities in the county. It also changes a fuel tax rule tied to highway maintenance and construction, and it took effect on July 1, 2025, or when it became law, whichever was later.

PA-2025-SB381.s: The law limits the use of state money for certain animal research, including painful studies on dogs and cats and devocalization, which is a surgery to alter an animal’s voice. It also requires some animal testing facilities to offer dogs and cats for adoption before euthanizing them, and it bars the sale of dogs and cats bred by people with certain federal animal-welfare violations. Schools and other recipients of state funds that use animals in research must also share reports on their spending, projects, and animal use.

PA-2025-SB398.s: The law changes the small games of chance rules for fire companies and club licensees. It lets fire companies with a valid license run online raffles, with tickets bought by debit or credit card, and limits them to two online raffles a year. This part of the law expires on December 31, 2026. It was approved and became Act No. 93 of 2026.

PA-2025-SB509.s: The bill would let local police use RADAR to check vehicle speeds on local roads, and on state roads if allowed by a state agency. It would set new speed rules, add fines for speeding, and require warning signs, training, and a marked police vehicle before RADAR use. It would also limit how much money towns can keep from these fines and require audits of that money.

PA-2025-SB806.s: This law updates Pennsylvania’s consumer protection rules by saying that people who make or share AI-generated content must clearly say it was made using artificial intelligence. The disclosure must be easy to notice and shown in the same form as the content, such as text, images, audio, or video. It also defines artificial intelligence and sets rules for what counts as a clear and visible disclosure. The law took effect 60 days after enactment.

PA-2025-SB807.s: The bill would change Pennsylvania’s Older Adults Protective Services Act and create an Older Adult Abuse Registry. It would require the state to keep profiles and case files for some workers tied to alleged or proven abuse, neglect, exploitation, abandonment, or related crimes against older adults, and let facilities and temporary health care agencies check the registry. It would also raise some penalties for failures to comply or report abuse, and require suspension or termination in some cases.

PA-2025-SB908.s: The law updates Pennsylvania’s Prevailing Wage Act for public works projects. It adds rules for custom fabrication, which is off-site work made for a specific project, and says those workers must be paid the same prevailing wage used for the project. It also makes firms doing custom fabrication follow the same reporting, compliance, and penalty rules as other contractors, and it took effect 60 days after passage.

PA-2025-SB922.s: This law changes the rules for private academic school licenses in Pennsylvania. It lets some schools apply before they have a building lease or final staff hired, if they include a plan and staffing projections, and it allows a short, temporary license approval for up to six months while some items are still pending. It also requires new rules for teacher and staff qualifications within 12 months and takes effect in 60 days.

PA-2025-SR400.s: The resolution would urge Congress to set 18-year active service terms for U.S. Supreme Court justices. It would also call for those terms to be staggered so a vacancy opens every two years, and for justices who finish a term to move to senior status, which means a lighter judicial role. It would ask Pennsylvania's members of Congress to support and advance the change.

PA-2025-SR401.s: This resolution would designate the week of October 19 through 23, 2026, as "School Bus Safety Week" in Pennsylvania. It would also urge motorists, parents, and students to follow traffic rules around school buses and help keep children safe. The resolution would also thank Pennsylvania school bus drivers for getting students to and from school and related activities safely and on time.

PA-2025-SR402.s: A Senate resolution would recognize and congratulate the Pennsylvania Chamber of Business and Industry for being named the 2026 State Chamber of the Year by the National Association of State Chambers. It also would commend the group for its work on issues like tax reform, permitting, workforce development, energy, and infrastructure. The resolution affects the chamber and its work on behalf of Pennsylvania businesses.

PA-2025-SR405.s: The Senate would honor Richard "Dick" Knoebel and express condolences to his family after his death at age 87. He led Knoebels Amusement Resort and also served in the Marine Corps, among other roles. The resolution is a formal statement of respect from the Senate.

PA-2025-SR406.s: This resolution would have the Senate recognize October 20, 2026, as "Pennsylvania Career Awareness Day" in Pennsylvania. A resolution is a formal statement by lawmakers and does not create a law.

PA-2025-SR408.s: The Senate resolution would recognize November 17, 2026, as "Pennsylvania Veterans Day of Caring" in Pennsylvania. It would also encourage residents to support veterans through kind acts, community involvement, and ongoing help. The focus is on Pennsylvania veterans and the people who choose to take part.

PA-2025-SR409.s: The resolution urges the Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission to review and approve adding the American Paddlefish to a state list that allows regulated fish breeding and stocking. It would affect the commission and those who work on fish propagation and stocking in Pennsylvania waters. The text says the goal is to support conservation and fisheries management.

PA-2025-SR410.s: The Senate resolution would recognize September 7, 2026, as "Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy Awareness Day" in Pennsylvania. It would honor children with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, including Decker Murphy, and note the work of advocacy groups and nonprofits that support families and research. It would also encourage people across the state to help raise awareness of this rare muscle disease.

PA-2025-SR411.s: The resolution would name November 2026 as "Good Samaritan Law Awareness Month" in Pennsylvania. It would also encourage state and local government branches to raise awareness of the state's Good Samaritan laws, which give some protection to people who report a drug overdose.

PA-2025-SR412.s: The Senate resolution would direct the Legislative Budget and Finance Committee to audit pharmacy benefit arrangements in Pennsylvania’s Medical Assistance managed care program. It would look at public spending, payment details, state oversight, and how well people can get pharmacy care. The committee would then report its findings and recommendations to the Senate.
